<insights>

- Low cohesion (0.19) — files are loosely related, consider splitting this zone
- High coupling (0.81) — 11 imports target "application-core"
- Low cohesion (0.19) mixing four distinct UI surfaces without internal relationships—organize MenuContent, OverlayView, SettingsView into feature subdirectories (menu-bar/, settings-ui/, overlay-ui/) to improve structure and discoverability
- Compat.swift bundled with UI components indicates platform compatibility logic is scattered; extract platform-specific adapters to a separate layer so compatibility concerns don't bleed into feature views
- 11 imports to application-core show this zone computes UI state directly from business logic; profile whether views are rendering pre-computed state or pulling raw models—push aggregation upstream to reduce view complexity
- SettingsView injects both Store (reactive read path via @EnvironmentObject) and AppEnvironment (write path and actions) simultaneously; this dual-injection exposes the full persistence stack directly to view code rather than flowing reads through AppEnvironment's coordinator, breaking the single-owner intent for Store
- SettingsView accesses store.schedules directly via @EnvironmentObject var store: Store, bypassing AppEnvironment's coordinator role for the read path; this creates a second, uncoordinated entry point to the persistence layer from the view layer and undermines the Store-as-single-source invariant
- OverlayView.clockText(_:) allocates a new DateFormatter on every invocation (lines 101-104); because it is called by a TimelineView updating every second for the life of the overlay, this causes one expensive ICU locale-loading allocation per second that a static cached formatter would eliminate entirely
- OverlayView.clockText(_:) constructs a fresh DateFormatter inside the function body on every call (lines 101-104). TimelineView fires it every second. DateFormatter initialization loads ICU calendar and locale data and is one of the most expensive object-creation operations in Foundation. Promoting the formatter to a private static let field would eliminate all per-tick allocation with no behavioral change.

</insights>
